articles.title_orig: Tencent, Visa deepen payments push in China after regulatory green light
articles.title_zh: Tencent, Visa deepen payments push in China after regulatory green light
articles.content_orig:
Tencent and Visa are expanding their partnership in cross-border payments and AI-powered commerce, the companies said Thursday, deepening their push into China’s payments market.
The agreement follows fresh regulatory approvals for U.S. financial firms in China, with Visa and Citi receiving the green light this month to expand their operations in the world’s second-largest economy.
Under the memorandum of understanding, Tencent and Visa will explore ways to make payments easier for travelers entering and leaving China while expanding their cross-border money transfer partnership.
The companies also plan to develop payment solutions that would allow travelers to pay participating merchants through Tencent’s Weixin Pay and Visa networks, subject to regulatory requirements.
They also aim to expand their collaboration through Visa Direct, Visa’s money transfer service, making it easier for overseas users to send funds into the Weixin Pay ecosystem.
The partnership will also extend to agentic commerce, an emerging form of online shopping in which AI agents can help consumers find, select and purchase products or services.
Dowson Tong, Tencent's senior executive vice president and CEO of its Cloud and Smart Industries Group, said the partnership would combine Tencent's AI capabilities with Visa's global network to improve cross-border payments.
"We hope to create more seamless commerce experiences for consumers and new opportunities for businesses, both in China and internationally," he said.
The announcement follows Visa’s approval from the People’s Bank of China earlier this month to begin preparations for a domestic bank card clearing business, bringing it closer to entering China’s domestic payments market after more than four decades in the country.
Visa and Tencent have been cooperating since at least 2019, when the U.S. payments company announced plans to allow international Visa cardholders to make payments through WeChat Pay in China.
Tencent has also expanded its partnerships with other global payments firms.
In December last year, Mastercard and Tencent's international payments platform Midas announced a collaboration to integrate Mastercard's Click to Pay and payment security technologies into Midas' overseas payment solutions, with the aim of making online transactions faster and more secure.
Last week, Citi said it received approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission to establish a wholly owned securities company in China.
The Shanghai-based venture, Citigroup Securities (China), will offer services including equities brokerage, securities underwriting, research and principal trading to domestic and international clients.
Citi said it would complete the remaining regulatory procedures before beginning operations.
The approvals come as Beijing continues to open parts of its financial sector to foreign companies.
CNBC previously reported that U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market access for Mastercard, Visa and Citigroup during bilateral meetings in Bangkok, citing a U.S. Treasury official.
The official said regulatory approvals were also part of an agreement reached by U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping during their meeting in Washington last month.

articles.title_orig: Fed leaves rates steady as governor Lisa Cook dissents
articles.title_zh: Fed leaves rates steady as governor Lisa Cook dissents
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Federal Reserve officials voted 10-2 to keep interest rates unchanged, as elevated inflation continues to pose a problem for central bankers. Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring a quarter-point rate hike.
The Fed's benchmark rates remained in the 3.75% to 4% range , as widely expected. A rate hike in December, however, appears far more likely, according to the Fed's dot plot and fed funds futures.
Here are the key takeaways from the Fed's statement and Fed Chairman Warsh's press conference:
Fed upgrades economy from "solid" to "strong": The FOMC updated the language in its statement, adding that "the accumulation of more information will help" it decide the right policy stance. This suggests the Fed is not in a hurry to ease inflation.
But "inflation remains elevated": Warsh reiterated the Fed's commitment to bringing inflation down to the 2% target. Although recent inflation data came in hotter than expected , the Fed has positioned itself to continue assessing data.
Warsh announces changes to the Fed's schedule : In 2027, one of the eight Fed meetings will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy with neither a vote on the Fed's funds rate nor a policy statement. In 2028, policymakers will hold two meetings dedicated to strategy and six for setting policy.
Warsh refutes the idea that the decision was politically inflected: Warsh stated that "politics played no role in the decision" — something that generated some discussion with the US midterm elections next week.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said he doesn't agree that Fed rate hikes will have no impact on artificial intelligence, given the strong demand for AI and the high returns investors expect.
"I was skeptical of that view," Warsh said during a press conference. "Interest rates get in the cracks. Interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything."
Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman, in a post last month on X , expressed skepticism that higher rates would reduce demand and investment in AI.
"What if higher rates don't reduce demand and investment because the demand for intelligence and energy is unaffected by higher rates because winning the race for super intelligence has a near infinite ROI and the demand for compute will remain incalculable," Ackman wrote. "What if the old models don't apply to the current paradigm?"
Warsh pointed to how credit spreads for certain assets have widened since the Fed raised rates in September, and financial conditions have tightened as investors have differentiated between tech firms and other companies to invest.
"With respect to the new technology and this investment surge, do interest rates matter? I believe they do," said Warsh. "And I don't believe that they're somehow divorced from the rest of the economy."
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh pushed back Wednesday on any suggestion that next week's midterm elections had a role in the Fed's decision to keep interest rates steady . He also dodged multiple questions on political topics and pressure coming his way from the Oval Office.
But it wasn't for a lack of trying from the assembled reporters.
"I appreciate the question, but I'm not going to be responding to quotes from public officials," Warsh said during a press conference when presented with criticisms from President Trump that interest rates should be lower and that his colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee were "political."
When the subject turned to the midterm elections, Warsh was similarly curt.
"Politics played no role in the decision," the chair said, adding, "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics."
Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban writes:
The Warsh Fed's taciturn nature has already raised the stakes for each FOMC meeting. With fewer hints or forward guidance about what the Fed is thinking and planning comes more suspense.
And next year, those stakes will be even higher as the Fed removes a rate decision from its calendar, making each meeting even more important and potentially adding another layer of uncertainty and volatility to markets .
At the October policy meeting on Wednesday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced this major change to the Fed's calendar and added that 2028 might feature only six rate decisions. The meetings themselves will remain on the calendar, but instead of the Fed debating rates, broader monetary policy topics will be on the agenda.
Warsh said the reasoning behind the schedule change is to "reserve the time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons."
We've all been wondering how the newly installed chair would reshape the Fed. Already, he's been doing that by changing the nature of the Fed's public communication.
Wall Street can't make up its mind about the Fed.
Stocks dipped after the 2 p.m. statement, rallied as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke, then gave much of that back. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) is holding a small gain, and chip stocks are doing most of the lifting.
The typical stock isn't doing as well. The equal-weighted S&P 500, which gives every company the same weight, is in the red. So are small caps.
The bond market is clearer about what it thinks. The 30-year Treasury yield is near its high of the day, and the 10-year yield is back above 5%. Higher long-term rates make borrowing more expensive for companies and homebuyers.
The dollar moved the other way and slipped against the euro during the press conference.
That leaves the streak. The S&P 500 came into Wednesday down on six straight Fed days, the second-longest run since 1994, which we pointed out at 2:43 p.m. ET. A higher close would end it, and a lower one would tie the 2018 record of seven.
Chairman Warsh said a couple of words on the Fed's independence amid some discussion that the US midterm elections — just six days away — and the perception that the Fed could influence them could sway the Fed's decision.
"Politics played no role in the decision," Warsh stated. "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics."
"But I will say," Warsh added, "it's an information-rich interval in the coming period, having nothing to do with politics."
The Fed won't be sitting on its hands for long, says the market.
Traders see about an 85% chance that the Fed raises its benchmark rate by a quarter point at its next meeting on Dec. 9, according to Bloomberg data. The data comes from futures contracts that let traders bet on where the Fed sets rates. Those odds are about where they stood Tuesday, before the decision.
Further out, traders expect the Fed's rate to climb from about 3.9% now to nearly 4.7% by September 2027. That's about three more quarter-point hikes, slightly more than they expected Tuesday.
The Dec. 9 meeting is next. A hike would match what traders already expect. Another hold would mean they've gotten ahead of the Fed.
Chairman Warsh noted that while the Fed waits to assess more inflation data, some policymakers view the central bank's moves so far as beginning to take effect.
"If you were listening next to me in that room the last couple of days, the overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgment, is that what we've done in this monetary medicine starting to work some, but there's no firm conclusions," Warsh said.
"If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today," he added. "What we decided to do was to call these questions, take stock of where we are, evaluate what we're seeing out the window, ask ourselves whether the period right in front of us is likely to provide more clarity on the appropriate protocol."
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced a change to the FOMC meeting starting next fall.
Warsh said eight meetings per year is the right number for the Federal Open Market

articles.title_orig: Tech Rally Stalls as Alphabet, Samsung Disappoint: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Tech Rally Stalls as Alphabet, Samsung Disappoint: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Datacenter and chip costs fueled sharp decrease in AI sector although non-AI stocks still had a strong showing
The latest shudder for stocks in the AI industry pulled markets lower worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran .
The S&P 500 fell 1.2% for its worst day since July, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 2.6%. The weakness for tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength for the rest of the US market, in which the majority of stocks actually rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11 points, or less than 0.1%.
AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build datacenters and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that their prices shot too high following a years-long frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.
Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.8%.
Other big tech stocks likewise fell following quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets.
Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, shedding tens of billions in market value, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it was creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.
Tesla fell 3.1% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.
The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4%. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value, movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single strongest force pulling the index lower.
CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1%.
The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where indexes are full of players in the industry. South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7%.
Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil leaped 4% to $113.17 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s shot up from less than $97 at the start of the month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.
In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4%. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or US indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds.
Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.
after newsletter promotion
Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong US economy and other factors, have pushed yields in the US bond market recently to their highest levels in decades.
But US yields nevertheless fell sharply on Thursday in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.
The yield on the 10-year treasury tumbled to 4.97% from 5.13% late on Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market.
Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the US economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country.
That solid economy has helped US companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the US stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. Two out of every three stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks.
Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.
CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expected “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.6%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 93.74 points, to 7,663.43. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11.89, to 52,867.98, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 694.00, to 26,008.86.

articles.title_orig: China-Japan flights lose nearly 700,000 seats amid political spat
articles.title_zh: China-Japan flights lose nearly 700,000 seats amid political spat
articles.content_orig:
Chinese airlines cut back the most as tensions that began almost a year ago continue to depress tourism
Airlines will cut nearly 700,000 seats from their China-Japan flights and axe more than 5,000 flights for the coming winter travel season as a nearly year-old political squabble continues to depress tourism, according to aviation data provider OAG.
During the commercial aviation industry’s winter season, October 25 through March 27, carriers allocated a combined 2,871,270 seats, compared with 3,554,167 in the same season last year, OAG data showed.
The same airlines allocated 3,889,781 seats in the six months just ended, representing a cut of more than 1 million compared with the coming winter. Summer is traditionally a busier time of year for airlines.

Lumentum produces advanced lasers and high-speed optical components that allow data centers to transmit massive volumes of information between servers with minimal latency. The negotiations could signal an acceleration in consolidation among hardware suppliers seeking operational scale amid historic enterprise capital spending on AI infrastructure. If completed, the combination would position Marvell as a more comprehensive silicon and optics powerhouse, though the immediate after-hours decline highlights market caution around valuation, execution, and potential regulatory scrutiny.

The company best known for its cute characters cut ties with the drama after strong Chinese criticism of its evocation of wartime torture
In an official statement released late on Wednesday evening, the company acknowledged that the Japanese spy drama contained content that “does not align with the Sanrio Group’s corporate philosophy”.
The controversial series includes scenes depicting Chinese intelligence agents torturing Japanese operatives, prompting China’s state broadcaster CCTV to accuse the show of distorting history and “deliberately smearing” Beijing.
In its statement, Sanrio confirmed that it was ceasing the current collaboration with Vivant – which premiered in 2023 and opened its second season in July – along with all related future projects and promotional campaigns.

articles.title_orig: Drones strike a container ship off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast and its crew members are rescued
articles.title_zh: Drones strike a container ship off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast and its crew members are rescued
articles.content_orig:
By The Maritime Executive 2026-10-28 14:37:17
A Greek-owned containership operating a route for Zim was struck off Bulgaria midday on Wednesday, October 28, with the Bulgarian Navy rescuing the crew. The latest attack on commercial shipping in the western Black Sea came as the ministers from Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey were meeting to coordinate their security efforts.
The ministers issued a statement calling for “an immediate halt to attacks that threaten commercial vessels, maritime infrastructure, and the safety of maritime activities.” They said they believe the risks grow each day and said they were committed to working together to increase security.
Evidence of the increased risks was announced by the Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov, who reported that a rescue operation was underway in the Black Sea. He said that a French maritime patrol aircraft flying over the western part of the Black Sea had provided information to the Naval forces’ operation center. Reuters reported yesterday that France had relocated its Atlantique 2 maritime patrol aircraft to an air base in Romania as of October 18 and it would be conducting surveillance missions until November 6.
The Bulgarian Navy reports that the containership Contship Jet was struck by a surface drone at approximately noon while the vessel was 17 miles east of Cape Kaliakra near Varna. The Navy sent three vessels, along with one vessel from the Border Police. Reports say the 18,000 dwt containership was struck by three drones, which started a fire and left the vessel with a heavy list.
The Navy evacuated eight seafarers and located 10 others who were in the ship’s lifeboat. They were all in good condition and transferred to Varna. Four of the crewmembers are reported to be Ukrainians and 14 from the Philippines.
The Contship Jet was built in 2007 and has a capacity for 1,276 TEU. It is registered in Liberia and has been operating for Contships Management of Greece since 2019. It is listed as operating on the Levant – Black Sea Express route for ZIM and was coming from Ashdod and Haifa, Israel. It makes stops in Romania and Bulgaria before a stop in Egypt on the return voyage. It was reported to be carrying 421 containers.
Speaking to the media after the meeting in Sofia, Bulgaria, the ministers said, “To date, numerous commercial vessels have been attacked by the parties in the Black Sea, while drifting mines, unmanned surface vessels (USVs) and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that went out of control or were struck, as well as missile debris, have been destroyed.”
Reports indicate that the Contship Jet was the ninth vessel struck since the start of October in the western Black Sea. Reuters reports that a total of 34 sailors have been killed or are missing from these attacks.
Get the latest maritime news delivered to your inbox daily.
Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey agreed to a series of coordination steps, including strengthening intelligence sharing and improving early warning systems. Turkey’s National Defense Minister Yasar Guler said his country also reserves all its legal rights and might pursue legal action concerning the attacks on Turkish-flagged or operated vessels.
Bulgarian officials also said that they were monitoring the capsized vessel Khoryv (IMO 8138712) as it drifted into the country’s waters. The Comoros-flagged ship (3,280 dtw) was struck on October 23, killing one crewmember, leaving three missing, and nine rescued by the Romanians. Bulgaria warned the vessel was drifting into its zone, and its navy was planning to inspect the wreck. Today, the maritime authorities issued a warning to remain at least half a nautical mile from the ship, which is now 13 nautical miles east of Cape Sivri Burun in northernmost Bulgaria and drifting to the southwest. Bulgaria said it is prepared to act if the wreck continues to approach its shores.

articles.title_orig: Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
articles.title_zh: Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
articles.content_orig:

Hundreds of World War I -era bombs, grenades and artillery shells have been uncovered by the melting of ice in Italy’s Dolomite mountains, the Italian army reports.
Weapons used by the Italian and Austrian armies during the bitterly fought White War in the region, were found in September after a period of sustained glacial ice melt.
The latest finds follow an even bigger tranche of ordnance discovered during the melting over the summer.
In a statement, Italian Army officials said: "As the ice retreats, history resurfaces - and with it, dangers from the past. More than a century later, the mountains continue to yield unexploded ordnance from the Great War."
It's expected that as climate change further melts the Dolomites glaciers , more of the White War's dangerous legacy will emerge.
The officials added: "These complex operations-carried out amidst melting glaciers, steep slopes, and high-altitude terrain-demand a high level of technical expertise and experience.
"Clearing these areas means eliminating hidden dangers and making the trails-frequented every year by mountaineers, hikers, and tourists-safer."
The "White War" was fought between Italian and Austro-Hungarian forces in the freezing, rugged mountain terrain between 1915 and 1918. It included some of the most horrific conditions of the First World War, as troops dug into defensive positions and endured extreme cold amid snow-covered peaks, glaciers and steep mountain slopes.
Hikers reported several sightings of unexploded bombs during the summer, mainly around Canal San Bovo in the Primiero Valley, in the eastern Trentino region.
The Italian army subsequently carried out searches across several high-altitude areas of Trentino-Alto Adige, where retreating glaciers and melting snow have exposed wartime explosives.
Recent operations have focused on the Care Alto and Vedretta di Lares areas of the Adamello-Brenta region in Trento, as well as Val Martello and the Stelvio area in Bolzano.
The army said munitions had also been found at Cima Tre Cannoni and along the edges of the Livrio glacier.
The army said the work aimed to make mountain environments safer for mountaineers, hikers and tourists.
The White War was fought at high altitude, where troops endured extreme cold and faced the challenges of snow-covered peaks, glaciers and steep mountain slopes.
More than a century later, the retreat of glaciers is exposing remnants of the conflict, including unexploded ordnance that can pose a danger to people exploring the mountains.
The army said the risks were not always immediately visible and tended to increase with altitude.
Its campaign to locate and neutralise unexploded munitions in the region is continuing as melting ice reveals further wartime remains.

articles.title_zh: A US cruise ship suspends a global voyage in Asia due to fuel costs, stranding 200 passengers
articles.content_orig:
A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Heng Sinith)
A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Heng Sinith)
A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Heng Sinith)
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia (AP) — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year voyage in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to “make the Odyssey your permanent home,” with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees” while it tries to restructure.
“The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements,” it said.
Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.
Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.
“We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything,” she said. “We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement.”
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn’t outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
“I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it’s a dream to live on the ship and I don’t want it to end,” Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn’t need to use a cane to walk anymore. “You come to this ship to live … it’s just sad that it’s all over.”
Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship’s woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn’t regret her investment.
“Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money’s worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising,” she said.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship’s operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia’s then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.
Associated Press writers Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and Grant Peck in Bangkok contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration sanctions North Korean network accused of infiltrating US companies
articles.title_zh: Trump administration sanctions North Korean network accused of infiltrating US companies
articles.content_orig:
'The Big Money Show' panelists break down the feud between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren as he fires back at her regarding her letters on bond yields.
The Trump administration imposed new sanctions Wednesday targeting a North Korean government-run scheme that the Treasury Department says uses fraudulent identities to place IT workers inside legitimate U.S. companies and funnel their earnings toward Pyongyang's weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programs.
Ten individuals and one entity accused of helping operate or finance the schemes were sanctioned by the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).
According to Treasury, the workers allegedly used stolen identities , fraudulent documents and fake personas to obtain legitimate technology jobs in the U.S. and allied countries.
"The North Korean regime continues targeting and exploiting American companies through fraudulent activities conducted by its overseas IT operatives, who weaponize sensitive data and extort businesses for substantial payments," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.
SCOTT BESSENT SAYS IRAN'S ECONOMY IS 'COLLAPSING' AS TREASURY TIGHTENS FINANCIAL VISE
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced sanctions targeting individuals and an entity accused of facilitating a North Korean IT worker fraud scheme involving American businesses. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images / Getty Images)
"Under President Trump’s leadership, Treasury will continue to use all available tools to protect U.S. businesses from these malicious activities and hold those responsible accountable," he continued.
According to Treasury, the scheme involved North Korean workers concealing their identities and nationalities to secure jobs with legitimate businesses.
Once employed, the regime allegedly collected most of their wages, generating hundreds of millions of dollars that Treasury says helped finance North Korea's weapons programs.
The new sanctions target individuals and an entity accused of sustaining the schemes on behalf of the North Korean government.
QUEST DIAGNOSTICS CONFIRMS PATIENT INFORMATION ACCESSED IN CYBERATTACK, SYSTEMS TEMPORARILY SHUT DOWN
The Treasury Department says North Korea has used overseas IT workers operating under false identities to generate revenue for the regime's weapons programs. (Budrul Chukrut/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Treasury also said North Korean IT workers deployed malware, stole sensitive data and proprietary information and extorted companies, posing risks to businesses worldwide.
The networks have used cryptocurrency , sophisticated money-laundering techniques and artificial intelligence tools to generate and transfer funds for the North Korean government, according to Treasury.
Among the sanctioned individuals is Russian intermediary Vitold Viktorovich Obertas, who allegedly handled nearly $2 million in cryptocurrency conversions and at least $1.25 million in other currency transactions for North Korean officials since January 2025.
Another Russian national, Ilya Aleksandrovich Boykov, allegedly supported a previously sanctioned North Korean entity by facilitating cryptocurrency transactions worth the equivalent of $3.5 million since 2024.
Treasury said the First Financial and Technical Development Center, a North Korean-controlled entity located in Russia, deployed highly trained North Korean IT workers who allegedly employed "Super Intelligence (SI) tools" and sophisticated money-laundering methods, including complex cryptocurrency transfers.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
President Donald Trump's administration imposed new sanctions targeting a North Korean network accused of using fraudulent IT employment schemes to generate revenue for Pyongyang. (Alex WROBLEWSKI / AFP via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Treasury previously imposed separate sanctions against another North Korean IT-worker network in March.
The sanctions block property and interests in property belonging to the designated individuals and the entity that are in the U.S. or in the possession or control of U.S. persons and generally prohibit U.S. persons from conducting transactions involving them, unless authorized by OFAC.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Iran rejects "unacceptable" ideas as Qatari mediators say they presented new draft deal to Tehran
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran rejects "unacceptable" ideas as Qatari mediators say they presented new draft deal to Tehran
articles.content_orig:
The master of a vessel on the Strait of Hormuz reported seeing another vessel on fire nine nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, on Thursday, a monitoring agency run by the British military said.
The crew's status wasn't known and there was no damage assessment or report on the incident's environmental impact, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) added.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Thursday it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the group at the kingdom's eastern region.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Eastern Province," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X.
Saudi Arabia has this month come under sustained attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport that was the kingdom's deadliest in years.
The Houthis said this week they had targeted the Ras Tanura refinery in the oil-rich Eastern Province with a ballistic missile.
Tehran has denied having anything to do with attacks by the Houthis after Saudi Arabia accused Iran of having encouraged the group's escalation against the kingdom.
Following an uneasy four-year truce, fighting reignited in Yemen in July, months into the U.S.-Iran conflict that has plunged the wider region into crisis.
Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem said Wednesday the Iran-backed Lebanese movement was not concerned with the results of Israel's election , vowing to continue its "resistance" against the neighbouring country no matter who wins.
With 85% of ballots counted, the right-wing bloc of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a slight lead over the main opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, but was still short of a majority after Tuesday's election.
"We do not concern ourselves with who governs Israel, but let it be perfectly clear that it cannot continue its occupation and must leave our land," Qassem said in a written statement.
"The resistance will continue ... and will stand up to the aggression directed against it and against Lebanon, and there is no room to discuss the disarmament" of Hezbollah "as long as the occupation persists and its aggression continues," he added.
The group, which once dominated political life in Lebanon, has been weakened by the two wars it has waged against Israel since 2023.
U.K. Treasury chief John Healey used his first budget Wednesday to offer households and businesses some support with energy bills this winter in the face of what he termed "global economic storms."
He said that his "choice in the budget today is to give families and businesses some breathing space now," as the consequences of the Middle East conflict play out.
"For families, that means higher prices at the pump, higher energy bills and higher mortgages," he said in his statement, one of the main dates of the parliamentary calendar. "For businesses, higher running costs and more expensive loans. And the impact is felt in the public finances, too."
Among the measures announced was a 100-pound ($133) one-off payment this winter for 20 million lower- and middle-income households, proportionately more of whom live in the electoral battlegrounds in northern England.
Other measures include the extension of a cut in the sales tax on electricity bills and the abolition of a charge paid on gas bills.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused the Arab parties of stealing the election through widespread fraud and called on Shin Bet, Israel's security agency, to investigate.
"We demand from the police and the Shin Bet a thorough investigation into the election theft by the Arab parties and the full prosecution of the criminals," Netanyahu's Likud party shared on his X account , translated from Hebrew. "This is a serious blow to Israeli democracy and the voting rights of Israeli citizens. The law enforcement agencies must act with an iron fist and in an immediate manner."
Netanyahu's party leads in the latest vote counts , but all of the parties will fall short of the majority needed to control the Knesset, Israel's parliament. With 85% of votes counted, Netanyahu's Likud party has 20.8% and Eisenkot's Yashar party has 16.1%, according to official election data.
Local media projected 53 seats for the Likud party, 48 seats for the Yahar and other opposition parties and 19 seats for the Arab-led parties. In order to reach a majority (61 of 120 seats) and pick a prime minister, deals will have to be made.
Amid reports Iran had rejected the latest proposal for peace from Qatari intermediaries, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X that his country continues to review ideas for a diplomatic solution to the eight-month war.
"While our Brave Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the Homeland, Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed," Araghchi wrote. "We remain in close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week."
The seven-day plan was presented to the U.S. shortly after the U.N. General Assembly in September. However, President Trump rejected the idea presented by Iran for a seven-day ceasefire and then phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier Wednesday, a senior Iranian official denied Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal on Sunday, saying instead Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas , Reuters reported.
A source had earlier reported there were concerns Israel could begin a new bombing campaign after its election, according to Reuters.
Kuwait summoned Iran's envoy in protest on Wednesday, after Tehran denied one of its citizens, sentenced to death in Kuwait, was involved in an assassination plot targeting a top government figure.
Earlier this week, two Kuwaiti judicial sources told the AFP news agency that the Gulf state had condemned three Shia men to death for plotting the assassination of Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Fahad al-Yousef, collaborating with Iran; and for membership in Hezbollah.
Iran's embassy in Kuwait said earlier Wednesday it "rejects the Kuwaiti government's claim regarding the involvement of an Iranian citizen in a plot to assassinate figures or in any other act that could harm Kuwaiti national security."
It added that the person in question had been outside Kuwait for 10 years.
It said it regretted a "negative approach towards Iran, manifested, among other things, in the repetition of flimsy and worn-out scenarios concerning Iranian interference in Kuwaiti affairs."
In response, Kuwait summoned Iranian ambassador Mohammad Toutounji over the statement, which it said "constituted blatant interference in the internal affairs of the State of Kuwait and an infringement upon its sovereignty and the independence of its judiciary."
Abdulredha Haydar Dahqani was among those who had been sentenced to death, the judicial sources told AFP.
Dahqani, an Iranian national, had already been handed the death penalty in 2016 after he was tried in absentia along with 25 Kuwaitis. He was convicted of spying for Iran and plotting attacks.
Another was Hussein Abdallah al-Maatouq, a religious dignitary and secretary-general of the National Islamic Alliance, Kuwait's most influential Shia movement, the sources said.
Israel's defense minister on Wednesday denounced opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot for urging the military to resist post-election pressure from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has threatened new strikes on Iran.
"His call to senior military officials not to obey the directives of the prime minister or me or of other relevant security authorities, on the grounds that 'they have his support,' is an anti-democratic statement detached from reality," Israel Katz wrote on X .

articles.title_orig: Utah files criminal charges against prediction market Kalshi and company co-founders
articles.title_zh: Utah files criminal charges against prediction market Kalshi and company co-founders
articles.content_orig:
Firm calls charges, which include violating state gambling ban and profiting from illegal activity, ‘crazy overreach’
Utah on Wednesday filed criminal charges against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, months after a federal judge rejected Kalshi’s effort to prevent Utah from enforcing its strict anti-gambling laws against the activity.
The felony charges could represent a new tactic in how states try to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity, a clash that appears headed to a showdown at the US supreme court.
The charges include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity.
The state’s charging documents name Kalshi and its co-founders, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara.
In a statement, Utah attorney general Derek Brown said Kalshi has continued to operate in Utah, despite a federal court ruling that Utah’s gambling laws apply to the company.
“Gambling is illegal in Utah, whether you place the bet, run the game, or promote it. Calling it a ‘prediction market’ doesn’t change what it is, and being federally registered doesn’t put a company above the law,” Brown said in a statement.
The attorney general’s office did not immediately say what sort of criminal penalties it would seek in the case, although the felony charges carry the possibility of jail time.
In a statement, Kalshi called the charges a “crazy overreach” and said that “Utah is clearly playing politics”.
“We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona,” it said.
Utah has been on the front lines of a battle between states and the federal government over who regulates the markets. Litigation has spread across roughly 20 states, creating a fragmented legal landscape that analysts say will likely be settled by the supreme court.
Kalshi has maintained that prediction markets fall exclusively under federal jurisdiction and are not governed by state gambling laws.

articles.title_orig: Chinese boy who donated US$1.5 to end power cuts now works for energy company
articles.title_zh: Chinese boy who donated US$1.5 to end power cuts now works for energy company
articles.content_orig:
Feeling that his first contribution was far too small for such a massive undertaking, Wang quietly made a second US$1.5 donation shortly after
A boy in central China who donated 10 yuan (US$1.5) to the Three Gorges Dam project in the 1990s now works for the power grid, helping transmit the electricity it generates across the country.
Wang Yu, 47, works for the State Grid Corporation of China in his hometown of Zigui county, Hubei province, according to Hubei Daily.
In 1991, 12-year-old Wang received a daily allowance of just one yuan – barely enough to buy breakfast – at a time when his parents earned a combined monthly salary of less than 100 yuan (US$15).

articles.title_orig: King Charles shows off dance moves on second day of Caribbean tour
articles.title_zh: King Charles shows off dance moves on second day of Caribbean tour
articles.content_orig:
The King shook off royal formality and replaced it with some dance moves on the second day of his nine-day visit to the Caribbean.
Armed with a pair of maracas in the colours of the flag of the Bahamas, Charles joined a Junkanoo - a cultural event and carnival designed to celebrate island life.
Amidst the feathered headdresses and brightly coloured costumes in the afternoon Caribbean heat, the King, dressed in a suit and sunglasses, joined dancers at the front of parade to cheers from the crowd.
It was a lighter mood coming after the King's arrival on Tuesday where he delivered a speech acknowledging the pain of the slave trade, describing "the suffering of the past".
Speaking at an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth on Tuesday, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices.
Charles began the second day of his trip by paying his respects to fallen members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force (RBDF).
The King, wearing a set of medals and sunglasses, spoke with servicemen and women before he laid a wreath at the Flamingo Monument, which commemorates four RBDF Marines killed when Cuban MiG fighter aircraft sunk HMBS Flamingo in May 1980.
Later, on a visit to the Bahamas Boxing Academy, the King found young fighters and the head coach wearing an image of himself emblazoned on club t-shirts showing the King complete with a crown, gloves and a boxing belt.
"He loved it, he loved it," said Jermaine Gibson, president of a neighbouring boxing club who wore one of the t-shirts. "He said it was really good and we gave him one of his own."
The King watched two young fighters sparring in the ring at the academy which trains boys and girls from the age of eight to 18 years old.
"I might see you at a Commonwealth Games," the King told a group of children at the boxing academy.
Protecting this region from climate change is a theme of the King's trip and was the focus of his visit to the Bonefish Pond National Park. The site was once a rubbish dump but has been redeveloped and now protects 1,235 acres of mangroves.
The King walked along a new boardwalk through the wetlands to see the conservation work being done to protect this vulnerable, low lying island from climate change.
He met students carrying out field work in the wetland waters asking them about their exams and ambitions to be marine biologists.
"We've so been looking forward to this," said Joanne Smith, president of the Bahamas National Trust Council.
"We want more Bahamians to get involved in our national parks so they can use it to better themselves… we are so pleased to have the King here, this is really significant for us."
Then it was on to the Junkanoo, where the King could be seen dancing alongside attendees dressed in feathered headdresses and bright costumes.
The history of the Junkanoo is not clear but it's believed it emerged out of the slave trade when enslaved men and women were given time off to mark Christmas.
A small protest near the parade, which had activists holding placards with the words "Pay us what you owe us", was moved on by the police.
The small group of protesters were from the Bahamas National Reparations Committee.
The King acknowledged the "great suffering of the past" when he first arrived in the Bahamas, as he faced calls for slavery reparations.
Noelle Nicholls, chair of the reparations committee, said :"We are demanding an apology for those crimes, and reparations for the harm that was done."
Nicholls said the protesters' presence "amidst the pomp and pageantry of the celebrations... are for us also a sombre occasion, because this is the King returning in a way that has still not atoned for the sins of the past."
The King has confirmed that Commonwealth leaders will discuss the legacy of slavery at a major summit in Antigua next week.
The King ended his day with a garden reception at Government House in Nassau where he met Bahamians who have made significant contributions to public life.
In a speech, Dame Cynthia A Pratt, the governor general of the Bahamas who is the King's representative on the island, described her pride at Charles visiting the country for the first time since 1973.
"We trust that your time in our capital will reflect the legendary hospitality of our people," said Dame Cynthia.
"We pray that this royal visit further strengthens the enduring bonds of friendship between the Crown and the Bahamian people."
On Thursday, the Caribbean tour leaves the Bahamas as the King continues his visit in Guyana.
The trip has been planned alongside the governments of the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda with an emphasis on honouring the past but also looking forward to the ambition and possibility for future generations.
The King's engagements in Guyana will focus on the environment and biodiversity.
He will then visit Antigua and Barbuda, where he will be joined by Queen Camilla, for the CHOGM and his keynote speech as leader of the Commonwealth.
The biennial summit will bring together leaders of 56 Commonwealth countries to address shared challenges and advance cooperation.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft profits soar days after announcing thousands of layoffs
articles.title_zh: Microsoft profits soar days after announcing thousands of layoffs
articles.content_orig:
Technology giant Microsoft says its profits for the three months to the end of September jumped to more than $36.6bn (£27.5bn), just days after announcing plans to cut its workforce by more than a quarter.
On Monday, the Windows developer said it would offer buyouts to around 60,000 of its workers to cut costs as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence (AI).
Like many other major tech firms, Microsoft is investing heavily in the infrastructure that powers AI even as questions remain over whether such huge spending will pay off.
Microsoft shares rose by almost 2.9% in after hours trading in New York on Wednesday.
The recent financial results of tech companies have been closely watched by investors as they gauge whether the heavy spending on AI is sustainable.
Big tech companies like Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are expected to spend more than $700bn this year on AI chips and infrastructure like data centres .
Microsoft said on Wednesday that its quarterly revenue rose to $92.3bn - up 19% from a year earlier - driven by strong growth in its cloud computing business.
Its earnings were lifted by a 30% increase in revenue for Microsoft Cloud - its range of enterprise technology services.
The firm also flagged risks, including "substantial investments" in AI, among other uncertainties that could impact its finances.
The firm's chief executive Satya Nadella said AI development has helped grow the adoption of the technology and has delivered "real-world impact across every industry."
This week, the company said it would extend a voluntary redundancy offer to eligible employees in teams across Canada, India, the UK and US to adapt its workforce to "changing needs".
It will create "greater flexibility" for the firm and allow workers to leave with financial support and career planning resources, Microsoft said.
The company currently employs more than 220,000 people around the world.
Microsoft's stronger-than-expected earnings contrasted with Alphabet, as the owner of Google disappointed investors with its financial results on Wednesday.
The firm's shares fell by 9.75% after it reported a 25% drop in quarterly net profit from a year earlier and said it will continue to spend heavily on AI.

articles.title_orig: US should spy on Chinese firms to maintain edge in tech race: ex-CIA official
articles.title_zh: US should spy on Chinese firms to maintain edge in tech race: ex-CIA official
articles.content_orig:
Former CIA deputy director’s call to repeal Obama-era ban on economic espionage comes as Beijing rushes to protect trade secrets
A former CIA official has called for Washington to spy on foreign companies to help US firms stay ahead in the technology race, in what would represent a break from long-standing US policy amid intensifying competition with China.
“The US lead in many crucial advanced technologies is being contested or even erased by China,” wrote David Cohen, who served as deputy director of the Central Intelligence Agency under Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, in an article published by Foreign Affairs earlier this month.
“By abstaining from economic espionage, the United States has tilted the playing field against itself and magnified the Chinese threat.”

articles.title_orig: Weil Gotshal, Once a Legal Powerhouse, Plans to Dissolve
articles.title_zh: Weil Gotshal, Once a Legal Powerhouse, Plans to Dissolve
articles.content_orig:
Leaders at Weil, Gotshal & Manges, the nearly century-old law firm that worked for companies from the Lehman Brothers to General Motors, recommended on Wednesday that the firm shut down.
“Following a careful review of strategic alternatives, the Firm’s Management Committee has recommended to the partnership that the Firm pursue an orderly wind-down,” a Weil spokesperson said in a statement Wednesday.
The firm’s partners are expected to vote on the recommendation “in the coming days,” according to the statement. Equity partners hold stakes in law firms and can vote on company matters.
For over 90 years, the law firm was well-known through Wall Street for steering high-profile corporate litigation such as bankruptcies and mergers. Weil advised the Lehman Brothers during the 2008 financial crisis, and the firm claims it brought General Motors out of bankruptcy in “just 40 days.”
The firm said it guided debtors such as Enron, whose 2001 bankruptcy filing was the largest in American history at the time. It also advised Microsoft’s $68.7 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard as well as AT&T’s acquisition of DirecTV .
The firm had been mired by an exodus of prominent partners, largely driven by competition from rivals, legal news outlet Law.com earlier reported . And a potential merger with another law firm, Willkie Farr, fell through this year.
Weil is announcing its closure without filing for bankruptcy.
The news sent shockwaves through the Big Law industry, which has been going through its own changes. Big mergers and acquisitions have led to more competition for top talent – and then there’s the looming dread of artificial intelligence.
Weil was founded in 1931 and employs approximately 1,200 lawyers in offices from New York to Munich to Hong Kong, according to its website. The firm did not announce plans for its employees or office spaces on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: Germany and other EU countries block von der Leyen's plan to give Canada 'associate membership'
articles.title_zh: Germany and other EU countries block von der Leyen's plan to give Canada 'associate membership'
articles.content_orig:
European Union member states have blocked a proposal by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to grant Canada a special status as an "associate member" of the bloc.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and several other EU leaders pushed to remove the term from a draft declaration ahead of a two-day EU-Canada summit beginning Thursday in Montreal, according to diplomats cited by the dpa and AFP news agencies.
Instead, the revised document calls for a plan to establish "closer ties" between Canada and the EU without membership.
The declaration was approved by EU member states on Wednesday evening and is expected to be published on Friday, at the end of the summit.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, von der Leyen, European Council President Antonio Costa and several EU commissioners are attending the talks.
Von der Leyen first proposed making Canada the EU's first "associate member" in September during a speech attended by Carney .
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
However, the proposal raised questions among member states because existing EU treaties do not provide for such a status.
Diplomats said several governments were concerned about the lack of clarity surrounding the proposed arrangement and insufficient consultation between the European Commission and EU member states.
Germany , France and Italy were among the countries that raised objections, although they broadly support closer cooperation with Canada.
Another concern was that the term "associate membership" had already been used in discussions about Ukraine 's potential accession to the EU.
Merz had previously suggested such a status for Ukraine as an intermediate step toward full membership. Under his proposal, Kyiv could participate in EU summits and ministerial meetings without voting rights.
Von der Leyen, however, used the same term to describe a different arrangement for Canada, a country that does not have a legal path to EU membership.
An earlier draft of the summit declaration would have allowed Canada to participate in consultations on major EU political and regulatory initiatives as an associate member.
It also called for the full scope of the arrangement to be defined by the 2027 EU-Canada summit.
Carney, meanwhile, played down the dispute over the wording of the summit declaration.
He said the precise terminology mattered less than the practical benefits closer cooperation would bring to Canadians.
Despite the disagreement over terminology, both sides intend to significantly deepen their partnership.
The revised declaration focuses on an "Alliance for the Future," a term Carney has frequently used to describe relations between Canada and the EU.
The initiative aims to remove trade barriers, facilitate investment and secure supplies of critical raw materials, medicines and technologies during crises.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Both sides also want to strengthen cooperation on energy, climate protection, artificial intelligence , security and education.
Canada could gain broader access to EU programs covering research, education and defense.
A new economic council is planned to bring together businesses from both sides of the Atlantic.
The declaration also calls for a study into the feasibility of increasing Canadian liquefied natural gas exports to Europe.
However, EU governments watered down several economic commitments in the original draft.
An explicit goal of deeper financial market integration was removed. Instead of promising preferential treatment in economic security measures, both sides now intend to limit potential negative effects on each other.
The push for closer ties comes amid growing uncertainty over relations with the United States under President Donald Trump .
Trade disputes, US tariffs and Trump's territorial claims have raised concerns in both Canada and Europe about Washington's reliability as a partner.
Both sides hope that closer cooperation will help reduce their dependence on other countries and strengthen their ability to pursue common interests.

Trump previously dismissed the idea of Canadian associate membership in the EU as ridiculous.
He also threatened consequences if the arrangement harmed US interests, warning that he could impose high tariffs or halt trade with Europe in several sectors.

articles.title_orig: Europe's youth take to the streets - they feel locked out of a promising future
articles.title_zh: Europe's youth take to the streets - they feel locked out of a promising future
articles.content_orig:
From Milan, to Marseille, to Madrid and in so many other cities across Europe, streets have erupted in colourful, passionate protests in recent weeks. While most started peacefully, a large number ended in shocking scenes of violence and looting. There have been allegations of radical left-wing groups sparking riots intentionally and reports of police heavy-handedness.
We've seen thousands rallying in Rome and Florence. Hundreds of thousands across France. In Madrid, an encampment of tents has occupied a city-centre square since late September. In Lisbon, tens of thousands of mostly young people marched earlier this month. Tear gas and water cannon were used on protesters in Brussels, after young men dressed in black, their faces covered to hide their identities, threw rocks and firecrackers at police. In Albania, demonstrators alleging government corruption are demanding that their Prime Minister Edi Rama – already 13 years in power – stand down.
This continent feels volatile, socially and politically.
I've spent years in Europe reporting from a multitude of demonstrations, both peaceful and violent. I remember well the ardent Catalan pro-independence marches of 2017, the desperation and Molotov cocktails flying through Athens' streets during the 2015 Greek debt crisis, and various outbreaks of violence in France during President Emmanuel Macron's first term in office, sparked by fuel tax and pension reform proposals.
But this feels different. Protests are exploding simultaneously across Europe and the majority of demonstrators – both peaceful and violent – are young. Some really young. Among those arrested, there's an eyebrow-raising number of minors. Over half of those detained in Barcelona scuffles last weekend were under 18. Minors were among those apprehended by police in Milan after clashes, according to Italy's LaPresse news agency.
Europe's governments, for the most part, have been careful to distinguish between looters and rioters on the one hand, and loud but peaceful, legally organised demonstrations on the other. The latter tend to focus around a particular cause. In the current protest wave, placards and chants mainly take aim at education grievances, social inequalities and the rising cost of living – though each country also comes with its own unique set of complaints.
What has triggered this public fury in Europe's youth, seemingly so quickly? Are all these demonstrations in some way interwoven? And with major European elections on the horizon, how will governments choose to respond – listening to protesters' concerns, or playing the law and order card to win support from older voters?
Students have taken to the streets in France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania – a more than 1,000-mile span of the continent.
Demonstrations are often organised in an ad hoc way via TikTok or Instagram. Belgium's interior minister has complained about what he calls the "TikTokisation" of protests.
Student unions play a role in organising marches, but they are also inspired by the actions of peers in other countries, even other continents. Think of the so-called Cockroach student movement in India – a Gen Z social and political protest movement that emerged in May this year, starting with criticism of the Indian education system.
France, where the current wave of student protests kicked off in late September, fuelled by student complaints over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings, is a stand-out catalyst in Europe. There's a saying in neighbouring Belgium: whenever it pours in Paris, it at least drizzles in Brussels. The Belgian capital and the town of Liège have also now seen weeks of protesting youngsters.
In Barcelona this weekend, students were encouraged to demonstrate under the social media hashtag #InstitutsIndignats, echoing the French slogan, Lycées Indignés (Outraged High Schools).
In Athens, 17-year-old Greek school pupil Yiannis Papanikolaou told AFP: "School buildings are terrible and poorly maintained… I think something might change, because of what France is doing, France will spur Greece."
There's a continent-wide sense of economic malaise felt by large numbers of young people – and it goes far beyond education. They worry about the environment, and fret that AI will rob them of job opportunities. They fear the spiralling cost of living could prevent them from finishing their education and stop them buying or renting a home big enough to start a family.
In Madrid and in Lisbon, frustration has focused on the prohibitive price tag attached to housing. Portuguese Instagram-linked campaigns stated "enough is enough" and called on people to take to the streets as peers had done in Spain.
In Lisbon, Carolina ⁠Cruz, 26, a PhD student and biology researcher, said she faces losing her home as her rental contract nears expiry. "I'm the first person in my family to enter a doctoral programme and even with all the studying I've done, I still can't make it," she told Reuters.
It's an anger shared by 22-year-old Riccardo, a protester in Italy's financial capital, Milan. "Even if we don't manage to throw the country into chaos like in France or block every road like in Spain, the aim is at least people will start talking about these issues again," he told AFP.
And it's certainly not just young people on the left of politics who are angry. At the presidential campaign launch of French nationalist Marine Le Pen last weekend, young supporters described different concerns to me. Calling themselves the "silent majority" – not (yet) out demonstrating – they say they also worry deeply about "uncontrolled immigration" and safety on France's streets, as well as the cost of living.
The outpouring of discontent has spread beyond young people to include trade unions, France's disparate Yellow Jacket movement that protested against the cost of living crisis during Macron's first term, and other citizens' initiatives. This weekend, Kent in coastal southern England saw two protests, one for and one against immigration.
This miscellaneous mix of protests can seem confusing.
Mark Leonard, the director of the European Council of Foreign Relations, speaks of a build-up of cascading, competing crises in Europe, none of which have ever been properly resolved, he says. That sense of pent-up anger is now bubbling over onto the streets.
"One crisis layers on top of the other," he told me. "The financial crisis of 2007-8, the migrant crisis of 2015, the environmental crisis, Covid, inflation after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and now again with the war in the Gulf."
Leonard says different "tribes" have emerged out of these crises. Social media consumption and algorithms harden their differing perspectives, leading to a real sense of polarisation in Europe.
"We've already seen this in the US," says Leonard. "A sense of 'my crisis is more important than your crisis'."
Nathalie Tocci, a former Italian government adviser who is now a politics professor at Johns Hopkins University, tells me we shouldn't be so taken aback by the protests, or the youth engagement in them.
"We tend to think of youngsters as politically switched off and disinterested. We think they don't bother to go out to vote etc, but they are truly engaged," she told me, "just in a different, more grassroots way. Think of the "Fridays for the Future [environmental movement] across Europe a few years ago, or the demonstrations against Israel's actions in Gaza after 7 October.
She points to the student-led protest movement in Serbia, which recently defeated long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić in parliamentary elections. "It's quite something. They kept going and going, for more than two years. What sticking power will these new European street demos have? That's not yet clear."
And what about the looting and the violence?
Intelligence services in France and Belgium have described looting on the edges of legally approved protests as mainly opportunistic

articles.title_orig: High-speed train crash in Spain leaves at least 68 dead, dozens injured, officials say
articles.title_zh: High-speed train crash in Spain leaves at least 68 dead, dozens injured, officials say
articles.content_orig:
A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped in central Spain , derailing two cars and killing at least 68 people Wednesday morning, according to local authorities.
The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers continue searching the wreckage for survivors and bodies.
The crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, according to Spain's rail system operator ADIF. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Padilla told state broadcaster TVE the accident was between two high-speed trains heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville and that one ran into the tail of the other while it was stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track.
The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January. Padilla said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers were in the IRYO train.
"Today all of Spain is grieving," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.
Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.
"It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year," said Sánchez, who faces a national election on Nov. 29.
Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the crash was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Authorities were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track, Puente said.
"I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts," Puente said.
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focused on rescuing survivors and bodies from the most damaged train cars.
"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.
One passenger said, "We were all thrown into the air." He said he was "reasonably OK" but that his friend was in much worse condition.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
"We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."
Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood.
The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to passengers.
In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.

articles.title_orig: Putin: Russia in ‘close contact’ with ‘genius’ Musk over satellite networks
articles.title_zh: Putin: Russia in ‘close contact’ with ‘genius’ Musk over satellite networks
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk is a "real genius", Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday after revealing the two are in "close" contact about satellite technology.
The remarks came during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, during which Putin discussed Russia's own satellite internet project Rassvet, which provides internet connections to people from satellites.
"He's a genius, a real genius," Putin said of Musk, according to a translation of his remarks by the BBC. "We are in close contact with our American partners, including Mr. Musk."
Starlink is part of Musk's company SpaceX. The company did not respond to a request for comment.
Putin added that it was important for Russia to be in contact with Musk so Rassvet and Starlink satellites do not "interfere with each other in orbit".
"We and our American partners value this mutually, and despite all the political questions, we are working hard," he said.
Starlink has launched roughly 13,000 of its satellites, according to the company. By contrast there are only a couple of dozen Rassvet satellites currently in orbit, according to online satellite trackers.
The Russian Embassy in South Africa said on Wednesday Rassvet is "Russia's Starlink alternative" and "marks only the country's first steps in this field".
"Russia maintains close contacts with the US on space, including with Elon Musk," the embassy wrote.
Putin's comments about Rassvet and Starlink were made as the US and Russia appear to be growing closer, even as it approaches five years since Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Ukraine relied on Starlink internet in its efforts to keep Russia's forces at bay. But its military last week suddenly suffered Starlink connectivity problems, something Musk has admitted SpaceX did intentionally.
US President Donald Trump earlier this month said he'd struck a deal with Russia to import diesel in an effort to lower gas prices that have skyrocketed due to the US war with Iran.
Then Trump waived certain sanctions against Russia that were set to take effect.
Not long after, a US citizen was released from Russian custody, with US envoy Steve Witkoff referring to Putin as a "humanitarian".
Musk was born in South Africa and then immigrated to Canada before settling in the US. All of his business ventures, including Tesla, SpaceX and Starlink, are based in America, with most operating out of California and Texas.
The billionaire, and off and on again trillionaire, has been one of the biggest political allies and financiers of Trump and other Republican US politicians.
